scenario: AITA for being home all day and refusing to cook for my mom? | I'm a female in my senior year of high school and I have a younger sister in grade 10. As most of you know, schools have been closed for a while now and won't reopen for at least another month. My dad gets to work from home, but my mom still has to go out to her office. My school just started online teaching, and we've been getting a lot of assignments to complete. However, my mom expects us to make dinner basically every night because "we're home all day". That really annoyed me because yeah "we're home all day" but we have school work to do. I got upset and asked her why doesn't she cook, since she always finishes work at 5 pm and her office is like 6 minutes from home. Well, once she got home today and saw there was no dinner prepared, she got pissed and started screaming at me how she's so ashamed of us and how we're useless. When I explained how yes we're home all day but doesn't mean we have the whole day off, she got even more mad and said that it doesn't take that long to cook. I refuted by "why don't you cook then?" For more context, my mom is an awful cook. She literally puts no effort into learning or looking up recipes. My dad is an excellent cook. He's tried to teach her before, but she refuses to learn and complains. Before, he would cook for us almost every day, even if he came home late from work (he has a high demanding job so his hours range but he's home 6 pm the EARLIEST, sometimes as late as 9 or even 10 pm. + 30-40 minutes one way commuting). And what does he come home to? Either a low effort flavourless meal from my mom, or my mom sitting on her ass watching TV and asking him what's he's gonna make for dinner. So my dad is forced to make dinner at a late hour so he can eat. More recently, he would just eat fast-food before coming home because he doesn't expect dinner to be on the table. However, he asks if us girls are hungry and offers to cook something for us to eat because he's worried that our mom didn't make us a proper meal. I'm a good cook too (self taught), and I try to help out if I don't have too much homework to do. I did a lot of the cooking during the first 3 weeks before online school started, as well as baking lots of treats like breads, cookies, meringues etc. Also, my dad does practically all the chores in the house, while my mom spends all her time sitting on her ass watching TV. So AITA for not cooking dinner today and telling my mom to not expect dinner every time she comes home? Also, my dad ended cooking in the end today.

Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Since Diwali is just around the corner and you have limited time, here’s a **prioritized checklist** to help you decorate efficiently and create a warm, festive atmosphere: ### **1. Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). Her yelling might stem from **her own stress** (work, feeling unappreciated, or resentment toward your dad). - **But this doesn’t excuse her behavior**—it explains why she reacted poorly. You’re still **not wrong for feeling overworked**. 3. **Cultural Expectations**: - In some cultures, **women are expected to cook and manage the home**, even when they work. Can we take turns with Dad, or can you help with something else?"* - *"I’ve been cooking a lot lately, but I need time for my assignments. Can we figure out a schedule where we all contribute?"* 2. **Involve Your Dad**: - He’s clearly **overwhelmed** and **resentful**. Ask him to **help mediate** or take on more cooking/chores. - Example: *"Dad, can you help with dinner more often? Mom and I are both busy with school."* 3. **Find a Compromise**: - **Meal rotation**: Take turns cooking (e.g., you cook 2 nights, your mom 1, your dad 2). - **Prep ahead**: Cook in bulk on weekends (e.g., make a big pot of soup or pasta). - **Fast meals**: Agree on **quick, easy meals** (e.g., stir-fry, sandwiches, leftovers) on busy nights. 4. **Address the Yelling**: - If she **continues to yell**, that’s **emotional abuse**. You deserve **respectful communication**. - Example: *"Mom, I don’t feel good when you yell at me. Can we talk about this calmly?"* 5. **Protect Your Mental Health**: - If this **keeps happening**, you may need to **limit your involvement in cooking** unless it’s a **shared effort**. - Your well-being comes first—**you can’t pour from an empty cup**. --- ### **Final Verdict: You Were Not "Wrong" for Refusing to Cook Today** - **You had every right to be frustrated**—your mom’s expectations were **unfair, unsupported, and unreasonable**. - **Her reaction was unjustified**—yelling and shaming you doesn’t solve the problem. - **The real issue is systemic**: Your dad does **all the work**, your mom **doesn’t contribute equally**, and **no one is addressing the root problem**. ### **Score: 1/1 (You Were Right)** You were **not obligated to cook every night** when: ✅ You have **schoolwork**. ✅ Your mom **doesn’t cook for herself**. ✅ Your dad **already carries the burden**. ✅ She **reacted poorly** instead of problem-solving. --- ### **How to Move Forward** 1. **Have a family meeting** (when everyone’s calm) to **redistribute responsibilities**. 2. **Ask your dad to step up**—he’s clearly the most capable cook and should **not be the only one cooking**. 3. **Set clear expectations**—if your mom expects dinner, she should **help with prep, cleanup, or cooking**. 4. **Protect your time**—if she **continues to demand cooking without support**, you can **politely decline** and suggest alternatives (e.g., "I can’t cook today, but I’ll help with [X]"). --- ### **Key Takeaway** This isn’t just about **one meal**—it’s about **fairness, respect, and equality in the household**. You’re **not wrong for setting boundaries**, but you **should also advocate for systemic change** so no one is overworked. **You deserve support, not blame.** Would you like help drafting a script for talking to your mom or dad about this?
